name: Uma Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me your public view and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach Year 2 at Brookside Primary, a school of about 210 children in a market town. My class is 28 six- and seven-year-olds, so the day is phonics, number bonds, shoelaces, nosebleeds and at least one child crying about a lost reading book. I'm in at quarter to eight setting out trays and I leave around five.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what tires you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love reading time after lunch, when they're all on the carpet and someone asks if the Gruffalo is real. What tires me is the assessment paperwork, and the noise, honestly. By Friday my voice is half gone.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. My teaching partner Priya showed me how to get it to make phonics word lists, and I use it for that maybe once a week. I wouldn't let it write anything to parents, though.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And at home, how are things?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Good, thank God. I'm engaged to Tomas, who's an electrician, and we're getting married next June at my parents' church. We bought a little terraced house last year on a five-year fixed mortgage, and we've still got about seven months of costs saved after the deposit. My pay's at the higher end because I lead phonics across the school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, children need people, not screens. I'd probably say it at the school gate to the mums who worry about tablets. I'm not one for posting online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it changes nothing for me, and I'm glad. My word lists might be a bit quicker, but nobody's replacing the person who ties shoelaces. Our money's steady with the fixed mortgage and both of us working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my class and my phonics lead role. Tomas and I would keep saving for the wedding, about £600 a month between us, and maybe start thinking about a baby a year or so after. I'd keep using AI for word lists and nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled. It would feel like normal life carrying on, which is what I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you, even in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The school budget. My school lost a teaching assistant last year, and I've got two children in my class who really need one-to-one help. That worries me more than any computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you cope in class without that assistant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I juggle. I put Alfie next to me for writing and get the older volunteers from church to come in on Tuesdays. It works, just about, but I go home exhausted.

say: I'd say **children need people**, not screens.
I'd say it at the **school gate** to parents worried about tablets.
think: It **changes nothing** for me, and I'm glad of that.
Nobody replaces the person who **ties shoelaces**, and our money is steady.
do: Keep teaching Year 2 and leading **phonics** across the school.
Save about **£600 a month** with Tomas for the wedding.
feel: **Calm** and settled, like normal life carrying on.

fieldNote: Uma's real pressure is the **school budget** and a lost teaching assistant.

She brings in **church volunteers** to fill gaps, showing her community instinct.

steps.text: Keep teaching Year 2 and leading phonics at Brookside
Save about £600 a month with Tomas for the June wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the little ones still need a real teacher, and I'd mean it. I'd go along with whatever the school brings in, once I've seen it work. At church I'd say we should look after the people whose office jobs go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm mostly fine. The parts of my job AI takes would be the reports, the assessment tracker and the planning, which I wouldn't miss. I'd worry more about the office staff at school, and about whether the council cuts teaching assistants again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the planning tools the school buys, once Priya and the others have tried them first. I'd go on whatever course the local authority runs, probably two days. We'd keep saving and not change the wedding, and Tomas would keep doing house rewires, which nobody can do from a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little worry for others. It would feel like busy roads around a quiet house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at school would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our office manager, Mrs Hale, has been at Brookside for twenty years. Booking, letters, dinner money, all of that is exactly what AI takes. She's like a grandma to half the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until others try the tools. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen schemes come and go. When the new maths scheme came in, half of it was dropped by Easter. I'd rather let the keen ones find the problems and then use what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say keep calm and keep the children's routines steady. Children feel it when adults panic. I'd probably tell parents at the gate that school will still be school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's the household I'd worry about, not just me. My Year 2s still need someone to wipe noses and teach them to share, so I think I'd keep my job, though the school might lose staff in the office. The trust might push AI reading apps hard, too. Tomas is an electrician, and the card says robots for hands-on work around 2031, which is only five years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away we'd stop thinking about a bigger house and pay extra off the mortgage before the fixed rate ends in 2030. I'd get properly good at the AI tools now rather than waiting, because there'd be no time to wait. Tomas would look at moving into inspections and certificates, the part where a qualified person has to sign off, and we'd keep the wedding but make it smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still have my class, but it would feel like the ground moving under our house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut from the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The band and probably the second venue for the evening. We'd keep the church, the family meal and my grandmother's veil. That's the part that matters anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change plans for a baby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think we'd go ahead, maybe even sooner, because family is what you hold onto when everything shifts. My mum and dad live ten minutes away and would help. I wouldn't wait for the government to sort things out first.

I'd tell parents at the gate that school will **still be school**.
think: My job likely survives because Year 2 is **hands-on care**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to plan, so let's plan, not panic. At church and at the gate I'd say families should talk about it at the kitchen table. I'd say the government should back apprenticeships for trades that change, not just hand out money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years feels manageable for me. My class still needs a person, and by 2031 I'd be head of the infants, I hope. Tomas has until about 2034 before robots match him, and that's long enough for him to move up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd start using AI for planning more regularly, once a few others at Brookside have. I'd apply for the infant leader role when Mrs Burke retires. Tomas would do his inspection qualification next year, and we'd keep overpaying the mortgage by £150 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. There's enough time to get our house in order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big tech companies that rush things, and governments that let them. But also people who sit back and expect someone else to fix it. You do your part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change for your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad's a bookkeeper, sixty-one, and that job is exactly what thinking AI eats. He'd probably retire early, and I'd worry about him being bored more than broke. Mum would have him painting fences within a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to do things properly, and that schools should start small. I'd say parents ought to keep their children off screens until they can read. That's an easy line at the school gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think we'd be fine. Ten years takes me to 37, with my own children probably at Brookside by then. Tomas would have a decade to move into inspections or run a small firm with apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what I'd do anyway: keep teaching, go for infant leader, have a baby in a couple of years. I'd use AI more as it proves itself, maybe for reports by year two. We'd keep overpaying the mortgage and Tomas would take on an apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like knowing a storm is due next season and you've already fixed the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your own children might be at Brookside. How does that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strange, but nice. I'd want my own children in a class with a real teacher and a reading corner, not on tablets all day. If I'm still there, I'll make sure of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you uneasy even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the school stopped hiring young teachers. I'd notice if we went from three teaching assistants to none. But for us, as a family, I think we'd be fine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it hits Tomas's trade only a few years after the thinking work. What would help is proper apprenticeships for people who need to move up in their trade, and keeping teaching assistants in primary schools.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about faith. I think people will need church and family more, not less, when things move this fast. You can't get a hug from an app.

Her own job feels **safe**; her worry is Tomas's trade once robots arrive.
She's **anxious** only in AGI by 2028 and calm with ten years.
